From the uncomfortable, unappealing, ugly jig of the film's head-scratching overlong opening to the contradictory and incoherently paired quotations by MLK and Malcolm X at the end, this is an in-your-face obnoxious mess that has no clear idea of what it wants to say but is utterly convinced of its own grand importance. The film consists almost entirely of babbling losers spending the whole day aimlessly wandering back and forth on a small stretch of road. Almost without exception these are not characters but thinly drawn racist stereotypes of purposeless black idiots who are hell-bent on getting themselves into trouble but are too stupid to know how to do even that. What is supposed to pass for acting is way-the-hell over-the-top mugging by everyone except the bland and stilted phoned-in performance of the film's wannabe auteur director/screenwriter/producer Spike Lee as well as two fine performances by two of the film's three major white actors, the always excellent John Turturro and Danny Aiello. Lee loves his grandiloquent soliloquies, which consist either of lists or of outright plagiarism (or "homage," as he would dishonestly put it). There is a short montage of several actors one by one looking directly into the camera and each insulting a particular race; the insults consist of lists of nouns and adjectives; they are predicates without propositions. There is a gratuitously long list of popular black American musicians rattled off by Sam Jackson's radio host; the sole purpose here is to provide evidence that, despite what we see depicted in the film in terms of black people's behavior, many black Americans have been very successful in music; yes, that is as much of a non sequitur as it seems. Also shoehorned into the film is identification by name of to that point (1989) every black American political activist, politician, entertainer, and athlete; it is just a product placement-like in-aggregate information dump intended to serve the same purpose as the radio host's annoying list. The plagiarism is in the form of one mostly mute knuckle dragger's beat-by-beat reiteration of Robert Mitchum's love/hate soliloquy from The Night of the Hunter; it makes no sense that this individual would be familiar, certainly to the extent of memorization, with this cultural reference. This individual's sole mission is to be as irritating as possible by blaring his loud radio at everyone to provoke a response. It is all just back-and-forth yelling until a white character smashes the radio, giving this dude his pretext for attempted murder and Lee his pretext for showing the cops killing the provocateur and the mob its pretext to engage in wanton destruction. At this point the loosely knit mob of miscreants unites in its fulfilling its collective purpose of attempting to murder whitey, burning his business to the ground, and attacking the emergency responders when they arrive. These violent black thugs trying to commit suicide by cop invoke the names of real-life violent black thugs (Michael Stewart and Eleanor Bumpurs, misspelled as "Bumpers" in the end-credits dedication) who in real life did get themselves killed by the fault of their own similar recklessness. Is this hateful, insidious wreck of a movie really positing the perspective that these arsonists and would-be murderers are, or believe themselves to be, oppressed by the genial owner of the one place where they each go multiple times per day to purchase food, namely slices of pizza? What does "fight the power" (a phrase repeated about a million times in this movie) mean if not that? At the same time are we supposed to respond sympathetically when a violent mob of "fucking niggers" (to use Spike Lee's obsessively repeated choice phrase) attempt to murder the white man and then burn the place to the ground before turning on the Korean shop owner across the street and threatening him with the same fate for no reason other than that he is not black? The race riot scene is a sadistic fantasy of a racially inverted recreation of the Howard Beach incident (the mob in the film chants "Howard Beach"), the mythical attack of a black man by a white mob outside of a pizzeria in New York a few years before this movie came out. The myopic libs of 1989 America, and worldwide, were too busy drooling all over themselves and each other in competitive heaping of praise upon this work of fiction to notice or care about the world's largest democracy movement in generations, which was ongoing by the film's May 19 Cannes showing and which was weeks past its bloody finale by the film's June 30 wide release. This film's revolution around interpersonal bickering takes on a sobering context in light of the PLA's massacre of thousands, albeit thousands of miles away. The point is not that the film should be criticized with respect to an unrelated contemporaneous political event, but rather that the inordinately high critical appraisal derives not so much from a considered assessment of the film on its merits as from a conflation of the film's social consciousness with its artistic value, this conflation based in a paucity of perspective of the extent of that consciousness. At one point the graffiti'd phrase "TAWANA TOLD THE TRUTH!" appears very prominently, to put it lightly. Is this a commentary on the credulity of those who were still clinging to their desperate gang-rape fantasy, or is it a statement of sincerity? Just before the end credits why do we have MLK telling us (namely, black Americans) to be non-violent but then Malcolm X exhorting "us" to violence? Is the senseless violence depicted in the film supposed to give its community of perpetrators a sense of accomplishment for having driven out one of the vanishingly small number of businesses operating in their ghetto neighborhood? How does it make any sense that this decent guy would be an oppressor of any sort or part of "the power" to fight? The film has no idea about any of this. Like the rioters leaning in to their true calling of vicious hooliganism, Lee has heard of the names of some high-profile black people, many accomplished, some criminal, and wants to make a movie having something vaguely to do with them, but he got too wrapped up in the aimless wandering to care in the slightest about what his original objective was or where he was going, if he was ever going anywhere at all.

I was honestly prepared to give this half a star. Then the Martin Luther King Jr. quotation appeared at the end and, for a moment, I thought the film had managed to redeem itself. Two stars, perhaps. Then came the Malcolm X quotation, and I was back down to one. For me, this is a confused and frustrating film, muddled in its broader argument. The performances are strong, and the actors do what they can with the material, but the dialogue often feels artificial and overly constructed. Rather than emerging organically, the story often feels as if it has been built around a thesis the film itself has not fully worked out. My issue is not with the film’s anger at racism, police brutality or the marginalisation of black communities. Those are urgent and historically entrenched issues. My issue is with the way the film frames its central conflict, particularly around Sal’s pizzeria. Yes, it is an Italian-owned business in a Black neighbourhood, and that context matters. But it is still an Italian-American pizzeria. The demand that Sal place black public figures on his Wall of Fame is presented as a question of representation… but, representation cannot simply mean overriding the cultural identity of a space because it happens to exist within a different community. Yes, in the 1980s, the lack of black representation in American public life is a serious problem. But is the wall of an immigrant-owned pizzeria really the battleground on which that struggle should be fought? The film becomes even more troubling in its final act. Radio Raheem’s death at the hands of the police is unjust and horrifying. The police are clearly responsible for that death. But the escalation that precedes it is not morally simple either. A group enters Sal’s pizzeria aggressively, tensions rise, Sal reacts poorly, violence erupts, and then the police arrive and kill a man. That killing is the central injustice. But does that automatically make Sal responsible for what the police did? Was his business the correct object of retaliation? Spike Lee has said that only white viewers tend to ask whether Mookie “did the right thing”, arguing that the real issue is the difference between property damage and the death of a black man. I understand that distinction, and it is obviously true that a human life is worth infinitely more than a shop window. But that does not, by itself, settle the moral question. Property damage and state violence are not equivalent, but nor does the horror of one automatically justify the other. The question is not whether Sal’s window matters more than Radio Raheem’s life. Of course it does not. The question is whether destroying Sal’s pizzeria was a meaningful act of resistance, an act of misdirected rage, or something more ambiguous. This is where I find the film, and Lee’s later commentary on it, frustrating. There seems to be an almost absolute certainty about what “the right thing” is, yet the film itself ends with two quotations that appear to be in philosophical mismatch with one another. If the answer is supposed to be so obvious, why close the film with both Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X? Why invite that contradiction and then treat the central moral question as if it should not be asked? I would probably have appreciated Do the Right Thing more had I known less about Spike Lee’s own interpretations of it, and less about some of the troubling accounts surrounding his behaviour on set. Taken purely as a film, it has energy, anger and some visual confidence. But as a political statement, I found it far less persuasive than its reputation suggests. The film would be stronger if it allowed more room for doubt, rather than presenting moral certainty as though it were the same thing as moral clarity. The strongest version of this film would have understood that.

Spike Lee’s Do the Right Thing shows how untreated tensions can bring out problems that were already happening in the neighborhood. I thought the movie was interesting because the heat made everyone more angry and frustrated. One thing I noticed was the color. The streets had a lot of colors  which made the neighborhood feel very hot and intense. The characters were also always outside, sweating and arguing which made me feel like the heat was making the problems worse. I also liked how the music was used the loud hip-hop that played throughout the movie. It helped show the energy of the neighborhood and made the movie feel more real. The cinematography also helped show the conflict, between the characters. During arguments Lee uses close up shots to show people’s faces, which made their emotions easier to see. There were also low angle shots and moving camera shots that made some scenes feel more intense. My interesting character was Mookie because he seemed like a normal person who was stuck between different sides of the neighborhood and he tried to help the problems but By the end when he throws the trash can through Sal’s window I was surprised because it helped start the destruction of the pizzeria. The movie made me think about how people can make choices when they are angry. I think Spike Lee wanted us to understand that the heat did not cause all the problems it just brought out the racism, anger and tension that were already there. But overall i didn't seem to enjoy the movje the plot was non existence and i understand the message the movies trying to send. I wanted to like this movie and everyone tells you to because you see 5 stars everywhere and yes on a technical level, it's hard to argue that the cinematography is vivid, the direction confident, the performances genuinely great. Danny Aiello and Ossie Davis in particular are a masterclass in screen presence, oozing panache and charm and they've got that rare charisma where you feel their characters even when they're just standing around. But I can't get on board with the movie as a whole. Spike Lee never lets you forget this is a Statement. Every frame is turned up to eleven, the heat, the sweat, the sound design, the racial tension simmering into rage and by the midpoint it stops feeling like a story and starts feeling like a lecture. The film is soaked in anger from start to finish, and while I understand that's the point, it makes for a genuinely draining watch rather than an illuminating one. The ending with dueling quotes from Malcolm X and MLK, capped with the message that violence is bad. Thank you ….Groundbreaking. After two hours of escalating tension, the takeaway lands with all the subtlety of a PSA. I get why this movie is canonized. It's well made, it's ambitious, and Aiello and Davis alone are worth the price of admission. But important" and "enjoyable aren't the same thing, and for me, this one stays firmly in the first category….

The heat did not cause the problems on the block but it did bring everybody outside which brought all the problems closer to each other. As the day progresses the heat shows more and more through the warm hues that spike lee used and this correlates to the tension rising, when at the beginning everyone was joking with each other now as the heat and tension rises arguments begin to break out. His use of community and conflict also was effective because he showed how even when everyone is in the same situation their opinions of each other could be negative. One scene of conflict that really stood out to me besides the end conflict was between radio raheem and the spanish speakers, this stood out as effective because the loud volume caused me to feel tense, this seen between the 2 also showed community though at the end they were both able to walk away without any violence. To me the most interesting character was mookie, he was the most interesting to me because he showed the most change but not necessarily in a good way. Always do the right thing. Do the Right Thing is an interesting film, but its central message ultimately did not work for me. For about 90% of the movie, Spike Lee does a great job creating a lively, energetic portrait of a neighborhood slowly boiling over with tension. The characters are memorable, the style is distinctly late ’80s, and there’s a constant feeling that something is eventually going to explode. My biggest problem is where the movie chooses to direct that explosion. After a clear injustice involving the police, the destruction of Sal’s restaurant felt completely misguided to me. The restaurant becomes the target of anger for something it did not actually cause, yet the film seems far more interested in defending or contextualizing that reaction than questioning where that anger was directed. That becomes even harder for me to reconcile with the film invoking Martin Luther King Jr. (and Malcolm X) and the subject of violence afterward. I understand that the movie is intentionally presenting conflicting ideas rather than giving the audience a simple answer, but I still found its moral framing unconvincing. There’s a lot here that I respect from a filmmaking standpoint. Spike Lee made something colorful, tense, and memorable. Unfortunately, when a movie hinges so heavily on its social message, I can’t completely separate the execution from a conclusion I found fundamentally misguided.

Passend zum Wetter an diesem heißen Tag einen Klassiker nachgeholt. 1989: Spike Lee dreht frei und bereichert die Welt mit diesem (für die damalige Zeit) bestimmt sehr speziellen Film. Hervorragend: Musikeinsatz, Kameraführung, Kameraeinstellungen, Vibe und vor allem STYLE! Das ist leider alles, was ich an diesem Film gefühlt habe. Finde ihn hart überbewertet und kann seinen Status nur bedingt nachvollziehen. Fand ihn größtenteils langweilig und anstrengend. Viel Lärm und Geschrei (was wirklich nervt) um nichts. Und Spaß macht er auch überhaupt nicht. Entweder habe ich die Racism-Message oder die Kunst von Spike hier nicht verstanden, oder ich leide an Geschmacksverirrung: Dialoge, Darsteller, Story, Tempo … hat mich alles NULL überzeugt, nicht interessiert und emotional auch überhaupt nicht abgeholt. Und das sage ich als Slice-of-Life-Filmfan, der damit normalerweise absolut keine Probleme hat. Was Spike Lee aus meiner Sicht nicht schafft: die Kultur und das NYC-Black-Community-Gefühl auch für Menschen zu übersetzen, die nicht als schwarze Person in den 80ern in New York aufgewachsen sind. Das Schauspiel und die Szenen fühlen sich sehr nach Theater und „gespielt“ an. Kann es schwer in Worte fassen. „Künstlich“ würde ich als Wort wählen. Auch das Overacting fühlte sich seltsam an und das „wütende“ Ende das höchstwahrscheinlich auch emotional hitten soll konnte ich null ernst nehmen. Vielleicht ist alles, was ich beschreibe, auch exakt so von Spike Lee bewusst mit diesem überhöhten Stil inszeniert worden – dann haben er und ich wohl einen sehr unterschiedlichen Geschmack, was die Zutaten und Glaubwürdigkeit für einen guten Film ausmachen. 2026 hat dieser Film für mich leider überhaupt nicht funktioniert.

Spike Lee's film Do the Right Thing was a very good film that combined many different themes to convey an important message. Personally, I enjoyed watching this film because it shows very unsugarcoated topics that resemble issues that are still going on in the real world. The way Spike Lee directed this movie and the choices he made truly stood out and made this film special to me. Lee chose to film the story on one specific block in New York during one of the hottest days of summer. The way he kept everything in one neighbourhood makes the movie's racial tensions feel very personal. In this movie, I noticed Spike Lee uses a lot of close-ups to show characters raw and true emotions. In some scenes in the film, Lee has the characters break the fourth wall and speak directly to the audience. This makes the audience feel their anger, makes the emotions seem up front and raw, and helps us experience the frustration some of the characters might feel during similar events. I noticed the heat in this film doesn't create every problem on the block, but it does help bring out existing anger, racism, and frustration. As the day gets hotter, these things start to get worse. I also noticed Lee adds louder music to intensify certain situations. Da Mayor definitely stood out to me because he was always very wise and cared about others even when he was judged. Throughout the film, my opinion about him stayed positive because, no matter what, he always tried to fix and solve problems in the neighborhood. He is a bit of a complicated character because he drinks, but he is still always kind, and he always regulated the chaos with his calmness throughout the film.

Watching Do the Right Thing was honestly pretty interesting because I liked how the movie slowly built up the tension throughout the day. At first, the neighborhood just felt like a normal place where everyone knew each other and had their own things going on. But as it got hotter, everyone seemed to get more annoyed and angry. I noticed how Spike Lee kept showing people sweating, drinking water, using fans, and trying to stay cool. The bright colors and strong lighting also made everything feel even hotter. I also liked the cinematography during arguments because Lee uses close-up shots and low-angle shots to make the characters seem more aggressive and intense. The camera also moves around the neighborhood a lot, which made me feel like I was actually there with everyone. I think the heat didn't really cause all the problems, but it made everyone get angry super easily because I think it made everyone already in a pretty annoyed or bad mood. The character I found most interesting was Mookie because he seemed like someone who was just trying to stay out of everything, but he eventually got pulled into the conflict. I also started to see Sal differently as the movie went on because I didn't think he was completely good or bad. The scene where Radio Raheem gets killed was probably the biggest moment for me because everything went from people arguing to complete chaos. After that, Mookie throwing the trash can through the window felt like a huge turning point. I still don't know  why Mookie did that and that is one of the many questions I have about the movie. I also am wondering my Sal payed him after Mookie basically was the reason his store got destroyed. I liked that the movie didn't really tell us who was completely right because it made me think about the situation myself. At first I thought the movie might be be bad because there is no true plot line, but by the end I realized that the slow build up was important because it made the ending feel way more real because we knew so much about all the characters

I genuinely loved the cinematography in this movie. Spike Lee does such a good job making the heat feel like it is everywhere, even when we’re inside. I really loved the lighting in Mookie’s house when he lays on top of his sister. The way the room is lit, combined with the way everyone is sweaty and uncomfortable, it made me feel the heat through the screen. I also loved how Lee uses sound to make the heat feel even more intense. When the kids are yelling at Da Mayor, everyone is screaming over each other, and the scene gets so loud and chaotic that it almost feels physically hot. The heat doesn’t cause all the problems on the block, but it definitely brings out everything that was already there, like racism, frustration, and anger. As the day goes on, the neighborhood goes from feeling energetic and friendly to feeling increasingly tense, which made the ending feel even more shocking. Mookie was probably the most interesting character to me because my opinion kept changing about him. At first I saw him as pretty chill and someone who was just trying to get through his day, but by the end I was really confused about his choices. I also became more sympathetic toward Da Mayor because everyone treated him like he was a bum, but he genuinely seems like a nice guy and like he cares about the people around him. The ending was probably my favorite part because Lee doesn’t make it easy to decide who actually “did the right thing.” Mookie throwing the trash can through Sal’s window is understandable after everything that happened, but it also leads to so much destruction. That made me realize that Lee isn’t really asking us to pick a side. He’s making us think about how anger builds up, how racism affects a community, and how one decision can have consequences that go way beyond what someone intended. By the end, I wasn’t thinking about who was right or wrong as much as I was thinking about how complicated the idea of “doing the right thing” really is.

“Dago, wop, guinea, garlic-breath, pizza-slingin', spaghetti-bendin', Vic Damone, Perry Como, Luciano Pavarotti, Sole Mio, nonsingin' motherf-cker.” Do the Right Thing didn’t impress me as much as I thought it would. Generally, the film was just uncomfortable for me. While the culture and themes of the story are masterful, I don’t think I’d ever revisit it. The cinematography and mise en-scène stood out to me more than anything. The performances were decent, and it dwells into complex racial tensions without pointing to a single moral lesson, which left me feeling confused. The Dutch tilts represent and perfectly show the escalating tension and how everything is breaking down. They skew the perspective, reflecting the reality of a world going out of control, while putting the viewer up close and often low to sense the fear and power of a character. They do this with Radio Raheem the most as he is the biggest and sort of the most powerful presence in the neighborhood. The lower angles execute and signify power, giving a threatening presence and making one character look larger than life and imposing to another. Many people say you can feel the heat shown on screen and really blend into the environment around the characters, but I didn’t relate to that. The combination of reds, oranges, and yellows paired with the New York on location filmmaking produces this heat and atmospheric feeling. Cinematographer Ernest Dickerson applied this color scheme and avoided the use of most spring colors, while much of the production crew painted and redid the neighborhood to make it feel fresh, vibrant, and hot. These visual techniques communicated the idea of putting the viewer into the discomfort of the cast, but I felt like I was watching it and not really experiencing it. As the day moves on and the sun sets, the tension increases and the shots become more zoomed in and close up. Each shot slowly closes the viewer in as the day progresses. A few people have argued that Spike Lee’s performance as Mookie was the best, or that Bill Nunn as Radio Raheem was the best, but between all the performances in this ensemble cast, nothing came close to Danny Aiello’s performance as Sal. Not to be a hater, but most of the performances in this film felt unnatural and didn’t work for me. The way the film portrays the raw essence of a neighborhood and its environment through these performances is neat, except it’s not entertaining to sit through for me. I am a major fan of films that deliver a bleak and honest view of life, but this didn’t do that for me. An example that really annoyed me while others were impressed was Smiley, played by Roger Guenveur Smith . He was intriguing to have in the film, but the dark comedy he brought didn’t work for me. I felt wrong for laughing at him, so I never did. Amidst the chaos, his character is seemingly important, but for me it was just another reason to be uncomfortable and gave me a sense of blankness when it came to breaking down and analyzing the film. A particular moment that stood out to me was shortly after the riot, when Sal’s is burning to the ground and Smiley pins up one of the photos of Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. to the wall so that the community can have representation. This was one of the few Smiley moments that impressed me and actually followed his character through while serving a purpose, because mostly throughout the film he was just interesting to me. What I’ll credit the film for, and what I think is brilliant, is its themes and Spike Lee’s bravery to tell the truth in a way that very few people were willing to at the time. He forced America to witness and face the raw racial tensions that were a massive issue, and Hollywood preferred to avoid the subject and matter of these issues, but Spike Lee decided to prove them wrong. In the end, it became his magnum opus and a landmark piece of cinema for the future. Answering the question of what characters “did the right thing” in the end is complicated because after selecting through all of these characters, no one really did what was right. You could argue that Mookie throwing the trash can into the window was the right thing, and that’s what I thought at first when seeing the scene. But as the ending went on, nothing felt right about choosing either side or any character for that matter. What mainly brought the film to an uplifting and sort of rewarding piece for me was the final moments and conversation between Sal and Mookie. Talking about money, family, life, and sort of giving their last farewells really brought what the rioting and destruction came to an end. It felt like a peace treaty being acknowledged between every character even though the conversation was just Mookie and Sal. The film doesn’t give an easy answer to who did the right thing, and I think that is part of what Spike Lee wants the viewer to confront. The heat doesn’t create every problem on the block, but it brings everything already underneath the surface out into the open. Overall, Do the Right Thing has exquisite mise-en-scène and cinematography that portray the raw essence of the neighborhood, but between the uncomfortable performances and the lack of an actual story, it wasn’t interesting to watch. I never found it humorous other than with the three men sitting out in the sun once or twice, I never “liked” a single character, and while the music was good and the way the film is loud at all times was great, this isn’t a film I’d revisit. I need to read a big breakdown and have someone explain why this film is supposedly so masterful because aside from the immaculate themes and bravery in filmmaking, it’s average to me. After watching this film the thing I wanted the most, that I actual felt the heat in, was the scrumptious looking pizza.

Mi interpretación de Do The Right Thing : Buggin Out y Pino representan dos caras de una misma moneda enfrentadas entre sí, ambas radicalizadas, agresivas y buscando problemas donde no los hay. Esto es apreciable en que, por un lado, Buggin Out podría haber disfrutado de su pizza tranquilamente sin enfrentarse con Sal y, por otro lado, Pino podría haber tratado a Smiley de la misma forma en la que lo trata su padre en lugar de empezar un conflicto (en el caso de Pino hay muchos más ejemplos pero este me pareció el más significativo). Pese a estar enfrentados, comparten la característica de su incesante odio y búsqueda de conflicto. Dicho carácter es probablemente una consecuencia de la frustración que sienten estos personajes, puesto que Pino detesta el lugar en el que trabaja, Buggin Out considera que el mundo es odioso e injusto, etc. La agresividad compartida de estos dos personajes enfrentados entre sí irradia una serie de tensiones cuya explosión se recoge en la última media hora de la película. Estas tensiones terminan derivando en una espiral de violencia con grandes pérdidas como resultado. La mayor de las pérdidas es la vida de Radio Raheem, víctima de la violencia policial. Le sigue la pérdida del negocio de 25 años de Sal. Tras esta amarga conclusión, al final de la película se muestran dos citas con dos mensajes contradictorios: una de Martin Luther King en contra del uso de la violencia y otra de Malcolm justificando la violencia cuando esta sea empleada como defensa. Do The Right Thing no aporta ni pretende aportar ninguna conclusión sobre qué es esta Right Thing ni sobre cuál de las dos citas es correcta . ¿Acaso ha logrado algo la violencia de ambas partes? Una ha perdido una vida y otra ha perdido su propiedad más preciada. El final de la película se siente vacío de significado. ¿A quién debemos hacer caso, a M. L. K. o a Malcolm? Mi principal problema con Do The Right Thing es que esta disyuntiva está muy alejada de lo que vemos en la película. La decisión de Mookie de lanzar el cubo de basura a la ventana no es un acto de lucha contra el sistema, es sencillamente una mala decisión cegada por la furia del momento, ni siquiera dirigida a su verdadero enemigo y causante de la muerte de Radio Raheem, el policía que lo estrangula, sino a su jefe Sal. En la decisión de Mookie no se refleja la disyuntiva entre no violencia (M. L. K.) y violencia defensiva (Malcolm), es una decisión completamente irracional que no merece el revestimiento que le da la película preguntándose si hizo o no la right thing . La única conclusión que puede sacarse realmente de Do The Right Thing es "ojo por ojo diente por diente no conduce a nada", si bien esta cuestión y enseñanza lleva a mi parecer resuelta ya bastante tiempo. Creo que la ejecución de la espiral de violencia a la que conduce el odio, representado por la dicotomía Buggin Out - Pino y continuada por la confrontación Mookie - Sal, no es la mejor de las posibles. Existen varios ejemplos de películas similares que desarrollan esta temática de una mejor manera como es el caso de La Haine o incluso La Batalla de Argel . A pesar de ello, he de decir que me ha encantado la caricaturización de la comunidad cultural de Nueva York que hace Spike Lee y considero que es donde reside la originalidad de la película. Personalmente lo que más me ha gustado. El mosaico de personajes que la componen es interesantísimo y la película lo expone de la mejor manera posible a lo largo de los primeros 90 minutos. Esto es solo mi opinión y entiendo que haya personas que lo vean de un modo completamente opuesto. Igual estoy criticando la película más por lo que yo quería que fuera que por lo que es. Ya le daré vueltas. No sé si alguien leerá esta review pero si opinas distinto ojalá lo pongas en un comentario🙏

Ventiquattro ore nel microcosmo di un quartiere di periferia nero della fine degli anni ‘80. È una giornata afosa e Samuel L. Jackson nei panni di un conduttore radiofonico pacifista che inneggia al C-H-I-L-L ci accompagna in un viaggio attraverso le semplici vite dei vari personaggi che animano l’incrocio principale del quartiere, tra una pizzeria italiana e un ventiquattrore coreano: il vecchio ubriacone soprannominato Da Major, la mother prioress, tre buontemponi che vivono sotto un ombrellone, un ragazzo autistico che vende per due dollari fotografie di Marthin Luter King e Malcom X, un omone che porta sempre con se’ il suo stereo, un iperattivo ossessionato dalle sue Jordan, l’italo-americano Sal proprietario della pizzeria con i suoi figli Vito e Pino. Il protagonista, Mookie, è osservatore di questa bomba a orologeria (non a caso è interpretato dallo stesso regista). Troppo impegnato a cercare di vivere una vita dignitosa, non si schiera né con i bianchi né con i neri, cerca di salvarsi la pelle e di porre fine agli inutili battibecchi razziali che avvengono alla pizzeria, dove lavora. Man mano che la giornata va avanti capisce che deve prendere in mano la situazione e fare la cosa giusta. Divertentissimi i dialoghi anche grazie a una regia irriverente che cita i videoclip rap di quegli anni, montaggio serrato che non lascia spazio alla metabolizzazione. Lo spettatore cerca di restare a galla in un vortice di cose che succedono una dopo l’altra, proprio come il protagonista, finché la situazione non gli sfugge completamente di mano, e necessita di una scelta netta. Meno realista pessimista e più ispirante del suo fratello parigino La Haine, Do the Right Thing riesce a trasmettere tanta insofferenza verso la questione razziale con due ore che volano via grazie a un ritmo sostenuto e dei dialoghi - ripeto - divertentissimi (altra differenza rispetto al film di Kassovitz, in cui la narrazione viene arbitrariamente interrotta per dare spazio a dei “vuoti” cosmici, a dei piani statico-estatici che mettono in risalto un ulteriore momento in cui è scandita la vita dei personaggi: la noia). Per Mookie non c’è spazio per la noia. La sua vita è frenetica, americana, una miccia innesca un esplosione di violenza nel senso opposto.

According to me, the film isn't really asking me, Who is right? It is asking: What happens when everyone believes they are right? Mookie thinks he is right. Sal thinks he is right. Radio Raheem thinks he is right. Buggin’ Out thinks he is right. The police believe they are maintaining order. The neighbourhood believes it is demanding dignity. Do the Right Thing isn't a film about racism. That's so shallow, :This is a film about pressure. Spike Lee spends almost the entire film turning up the heat. At first, it feels almost playful. The colours are loud. The music is everywhere. The neighbourhood feels alive. People flirt, argue, gossip, joke, hustle and annoy each other. It is funny. Then the small things begin piling up. And that is what I found most disturbing about the film. The explosion doesn't come from nowhere. Spike Lee makes you watch the pressure accumulate. Everybody has a grievance. Everybody has a point. Everybody believes they are justified. Buggin' Out is angry because he doesn't see himself represented. Sal believes the pizzeria is his business and that he has earned his place in the neighbourhood. Radio Raheem carries his anger through that enormous boombox. Mookie moves between these worlds, belonging to all of them and none of them completely. And Spike Lee doesn't give me a clean hero to stand behind. That matters. The film's movement from comedy into violence is therefore terrifying precisely because it doesn't feel like a different movie. The same neighbourhood is still there. The same people are still there. The same heat is still there. Only now the consequences are irreversible. And then comes Mookie's decision. I don't even think I fully know what I believe about it yet. Was it an act of rage? An act of resistance? A redirection of violence? A terrible mistake? Or all of these things at once? And then I remembered something that made the whole thing even more interesting to me: Spike Lee is Mookie. The man directing this entire film—the man creating all these characters, tensions and contradictions—also puts himself right in the middle of it. Mookie is not some detached observer. He is caught between Sal's pizzeria, his community, his relationship, his son, his friends and the growing tension around him. And maybe that's why I find his final decision so difficult to judge. Because Spike Lee didn't give himself the easy role. He put himself in the position of having to choose. And then he made us sit with that choice. That uncertainty is what makes the film stay with me. Spike Lee doesn't let me consume racism as an abstract social issue. He turns it into a physical environment. A street. A business. A conversation. A look. A sound system. A hot summer day. And then he burns the whole thing down. Talking about burning; The heat. Everybody is suffering from it. Black, white, young, old—it doesn't discriminate. Everyone is sweating, irritated, restless and increasingly short-tempered. The heat doesn't create the racial tensions, but it becomes the environment in which those tensions are allowed to intensify. That's one of the things I loved about the film. The weather almost becomes another character. Spike Lee doesn't need to constantly tell me that the neighbourhood is under pressure. I can feel it on everybody's skin. And then there is the characterisation. Every role feels deliberately alive. The characters aren't simply there to represent opposing sides of an argument. They have their own personalities, contradictions, humour and flaws. Even the characters I disagree with are given enough humanity to make them difficult to reduce to a label. Buggin' Out is irritating, funny and politically conscious. Radio Raheem is intimidating, charismatic and vulnerable. Da Mayor is ridiculous and strangely wise. Mookie is laid-back but also deeply conflicted. Sal has genuine affection for the neighbourhood and the people in it, while simultaneously carrying attitudes that make that affection deeply complicated. Even the smaller characters feel like they belong to a real community rather than a screenplay that needs to move the plot forward. That is one of Spike Lee's greatest strengths here: nobody feels disposable. And because these characters feel alive, the conflict feels alive too. At first, we're watching a neighbourhood. Then we're watching tensions. Then we're watching people. Then suddenly we're watching consequences. The brilliance is that Spike Lee doesn't construct a simple battle between good people and bad people. Everybody has a reason. Everybody has a grievance. Everybody thinks they are justified. So the question becomes less: Who is right? And more: What happens when everyone believes they are right? The film's escalation is therefore terrifying because it feels earned. The explosion doesn't come from nowhere. Spike Lee has been turning up the heat—literally and socially—for the entire film. After finishing Do the Right Thing, I found myself looking for more Spike Lee. That's when I discovered that he also made Malcolm X. And suddenly, the ending of Do the Right Thing hit differently. Because Spike Lee wasn't only interested in depicting the tensions of Black America—he was also deeply concerned with who gets to tell Black stories, and how those stories are told. The making of Malcolm X has its own complicated history. There was enormous pressure around how Malcolm's life would be represented, including fears that Hollywood would soften, simplify or whitewash one of the most uncompromising Black political figures in American history. Spike Lee fought hard over the film's creative direction, and the project became a larger battle over ownership of Malcolm's image and legacy. That makes my discovery of Malcolm X after Do the Right Thing feel strangely appropriate. I started this film thinking I was watching a story about one neighbourhood on one brutally hot day. I finished it thinking about an entire history. About violence, resistance, dignity, assimilation and self-determination. And now I want to see what Spike Lee does with the man, the myth, the legend. MALCOLM X And so far, Spike Lee is the best social commentator I've encountered through film.

The Ballot or the Bullet? --- "Do the Right Thing"-- the colloquial definition might feel easy to say, and people say it all the time: "you should do the right thing and just..." The film asks: but what is the "right thing"? And how do we "do" "it"? Is there an objective, universal, capital T True "right thing"? If so, how do we get to it? It's one of those phrases I think we implicitly assume a definition for, but the film unsettles it so deeply that it loses stable meaning and reveals that the "right thing" is socially constructed and historically contingent. And it's really hard to turn back around and escape that fact once you fully and completely sit with it. It's like you've been looking through a glass windowpane your whole life but Spike Lee shatters it and only then do you know you've been looking through glass the entire time. --- There's lots to write about urban unrest, slavery's afterlives and permutations, the carceral apparatus, and racial difference, that I'm also sure many people have written about. Slavery under a different name, its vestiges hidden under a new garb, behind the facade of prison phone fees, predictive policing technologies, predatory debt structures, and dating app algorithms.

The music is great and versatile, not only from the same genre, and it has a lot of symbolism too. Lots of colours and culture too. I love how the movie is set almost entirely on one Brooklyn block, yet it never feels visually limited. It also has to do with the camera work that’s different than usual, especially for an 80s movie, but it worked so well. I also love it when directors break the fourth wall. It’s a little bit of extra experimenting and creativity that makes a movie quickly stand out. What I like most is the ending of the movie, together with the two contradicting quotes from Martin Luther King and Malcolm X. It’s a morally ambiguous ending, my favourite kind.

It's alive like no other movie and breathes like no other movie does. Not to take away from how important the issues it tackles are, this is hugely inspiring on a filmmaking level. It blows my mind that Spike Lee wrote, produced, directed and played the lead role and managed to make a movie with more energy than it knows what to do with. He must have been exhausted but the movie doesn't suffer from it. This feels like all of Lee's interests and obsessions synthesized into one little world. It can break the fourth wall mid scene only to go on as if it never happened. It has the greatest opening credit sequence of any movie. You feel like you know every character and have walked around this neighbourhood more times than you can count. It has a unique structure where it meanders around the block as if it's any random day, then destroys your soul, erupts into chaos and then starts anew the next day. If this was released as is today, I think it would be just as controversial. It's an entertaining movie but it's not an easy one. Even though I've seen this movie many times before, I'm never ready for how agonizingly brutal and unfair it is. The movie pushes you around like you're right in the middle of the whole ordeal and the conclusion cuts you deep. Spike Lee can't give us the answer but he can give us a dose of reality. What else can I say? It's not a simple movie but the movie itself is simply one of the best to ever do it. And that's the double truth, Ruth.
